## Operating model

The rule Etgar Bonar has used since Amazon: acquire the right customers, help them win with your product, and make getting value easier. Bring a person in when automation and mass communication are not enough, alongside them, never instead of them. Done well, the cost of serving a customer stops tracking the revenue they produce.

## Current point of view

The serviceable line is the share of the market, and of each customer's journey, a company can win without adding people: the work a customer's AI can complete with its product before anyone from the company has to step in. Where the line sits depends on two variables that multiply: how much work customers in that industry hand to AI, and how legible the product is to a machine. A customer's AI tests it with five questions: can it find the company, compare it honestly, work out how it connects, run the work, and recover when something breaks.

The serviceable line connects five current discussions. AI visibility, AEO and GEO cover whether a machine can find and cite a company. Agentic commerce describes customers delegating work to agents. AI agent readiness describes whether the vendor is legible and operable to those agents. Cost to serve and human escalation expose the economics. Service-as-software and outcome-based pricing are consequences when agents can complete autonomous, attributable work.

## Hands-on AI build

Etgar Bonar's AI build is the latest example of a career-long hands-on pattern. He has worked inside the commercial functions he leads, built websites across three decades, automated his home, and built a personal AI operating system at the smallest useful scale: one operator, no team, real costs and real consequences. The system connects AI to real context and tools, with scoped permissions, human approval, watchdogs, canary tests, backups and incident logging. The constraint it exposed connects directly to his serviceable-line point of view: where progress stops and a company still has to add people.
